meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but; so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

принимать.gloss: to receive, to see (visitors); to take

meanings.en: to receive, to see (visitors); to take
meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'нимать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to receive, to see (visitors); to take', paired with 'принять'.

examples.trans: The mayor isn't seeing anyone today.
The doctor sees patients in the morning.

examples.text: Я ему сказала, что сегодня вы не принимаете.
examples.trans: I told him you're not seeing anyone today.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'словие'). Common neuter noun meaning 'condition' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Look what the conditions are like here.

examples.text: Посмотрите, какие тут условия. В эту комнату, пожалуйста.
examples.trans: Look what the conditions are like here. Into this room, please.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'your', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, who are your rivals?
Tell us, when will your programme be out?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'game, play' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Это отличная игра! Хочешь с нами поиграть? Бери карты.
examples.trans: This is a great game! Want to play with us? Take the cards.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'chef' (head, leader, from Latin 'caput'); in Russian kitchen culture 'шеф' is the standard form of address for the executive head chef.

examples.trans: The chef is in the kitchen.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.
And does the governor support you?

examples.text: Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'there', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Abstract feminine noun formed with the Slavic suffix '-ость' ('-ness, -ity') from the corresponding adjective. Common masculine noun meaning 'guest, visitor' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Клавдия Викторовна, к вам гости! Па-пам!
examples.trans: Klavdia Viktorovna, you have visitors! Ta-da!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to call', paired with 'позвать'.
Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'hello'.

examples.trans: Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to want', paired with 'захотеть'.

examples.trans: If you don't want to, suit yourself.
They want to build a shopping centre there.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to see', paired with 'увидеть'.

examples.trans: I can see the toy car.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.
See the markers? They're from Japan!

хотя.gloss: even if, at least (with бы); although

meanings.en: even if, at least (with бы); although
meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'even if, at least (with бы); although', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Нужно хотя бы поговорить с ними.
examples.trans: We need at least to talk with them.

examples.text: Вы плохо поступили, но хотя бы совесть есть.
examples.trans: You acted badly, but at least you have a conscience.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'мнить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to remember'.

examples.trans: Do you remember the toilet in the communal flat?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'at, by; (у меня) I have', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to work', paired with 'поработать'.

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been working as mayor for four years now.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('young').

examples.text: Молодой человек, как на тест-драйв записаться?
examples.trans: Young man, how do I sign up for a test drive?

examples.text: Молодой человек, а как на тест-драйв записаться?
examples.trans: Young man, how do I sign up for a test drive?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'cook, chef' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Есть такой английский повар. Я по его передачам научусь готовить.
examples.trans: There is this English chef. I will learn to cook from his shows.

examples.text: Я хочу работать поваром в ресторане.
examples.trans: I want to work as a cook in a restaurant.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

examples.text: Разговорчики, лейтенант Соколов! Быстро на рабочее место.
examples.trans: That's enough talk, Lieutenant Sokolov! Back to your desk, quickly.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'over there', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'from, out of', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Марина Сергеевна, я уже знаю. Мне звонили из мэрии.
examples.trans: Marina Sergeyevna, I already know. The town hall called me.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.trans: They called from the Italian restaurant.
In the evening they went to a restaurant.

examples.text: Кстати, звонили из итальянского ресторана. Дарят папе романтический ужин на двоих.
examples.trans: By the way, they called from the Italian restaurant. They're giving Dad a romantic dinner for two.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian expressive spoken interjection meaning 'yeah, right', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'тоять'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to stand', paired with 'постоять'.

examples.text: То есть просто стоять и смотреть?
examples.trans: So we just stand and watch?

meanings.note: Agent noun formed with the international suffix '-ист' denoting a specialist or adherent. Common feminine noun meaning 'dry cleaner’s' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Зайди в химчистку и возьми мой костюм.
examples.trans: Go to the dry cleaners and take my suit.
We will gladly pay for your dry cleaning.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'we', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to pay, to pay off', paired with 'оплачивать'.

examples.text: Послушай, я оплачу весь долг этой женщины!
examples.trans: Listen, I'll pay this woman's entire debt!

examples.text: Он уже оплатил счёт в ресторане.
examples.trans: He has already paid the bill at the restaurant.

examples.text: Послушай, я оплачу весь долг этой женщины! Клянусь, весь долг!
examples.trans: Listen, I'll pay this woman's entire debt! I swear, the whole debt!

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'нять'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to understand', paired with 'понимать'.

examples.trans: Share it all equally with everyone, understand?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'can, to be able', paired with 'смочь'.

examples.text: Этого не может быть. Это наша история.
examples.trans: That can't be. It's our history.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'would', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.

examples.text: Юле бы дублёнку купили, Славику бы ноутбук.
examples.trans: We could have bought Yulia a sheepskin coat, and Slavik a laptop.

выйти.gloss: to go out, to get out

meanings.en: to go out, to get out
meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to go out, to get out', paired with 'выходить'.

examples.text: Я выйду отсюда через две недели.
examples.trans: I'll be out of here in two weeks.

examples.text: Я выйду отсюда через две недели. Я решу все ваши проблемы.
examples.trans: I'll be out of here in two weeks. I'll solve all your problems.

meanings.note: Prefix 'до-' marks reaching a boundary or finishing the remainder of an action (stem 'лжен'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('must, should; owe').

examples.text: Жадность, Паша, должна быть умеренная. Комнатной температуры.
examples.trans: Greed, Pasha, should be moderate. Room temperature.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'могать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to help', paired with 'помочь'.

examples.text: Так, операцию продолжаем. Михаил Михайлович, помогайте Лаврову.
examples.trans: Right, the operation goes on. Mikhail Mikhailovich, give Lavrov your help.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'he; it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Common masculine noun meaning 'man' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: У мужчины бывает не только жена.
examples.trans: A man can have more than just a wife.
This man is waiting for you.

examples.text: У мужчины, мальчик, бывает не только жена. Это моя девушка.
examples.trans: A man, my boy, can have more than just a wife. She's my girlfriend.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'oneself, myself, himself', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
examples.trans: I'll have a good time on my own.

examples.text: Николай Филиппович, простите меня, пожалуйста. Я сам не знаю, как это произошло.
examples.trans: Nikolai Filippovich, please forgive me. I don't know myself how it happened.

examples.text: Я сам не знаю, как это произошло.
examples.trans: I don't know myself how it happened.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'делать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to do, to make', paired with 'делать'.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: Prefix 'пред-' ('before, fore-') indicates anticipation or prior position (stem 'ложение'). Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'offer, proposal; sentence' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: It's a good offer, of course.

examples.text: Значит, предложение такое. Ты мне говоришь, где твои сорок миллионов.
examples.trans: So, here's the offer. You tell me where your forty million is.
